If you ever decide to research cleanroom software engineering, you'll probably hear about one company, Phoenix Technologies.

Phoenix Technologies was a company operating at a time when the PC market was exploding and IBM-compatible computers were becoming the industry standard. The company specialized in low-level system software—most notably firmware, including BIOS implementations that sat between hardware and operating systems.

Rather than selling consumer products, Phoenix worked behind the scenes. Its software was licensed by computer manufacturers around the world and shipped on millions of machines, making it a pretty influential company in the PC ecosystem despite having very little public visibility.

And Pheonix... they didn't give a shit about innovation or cutting edge product features. They knew their customers would have just as compelling of a motherboard as IBM had if it could run all the same software.

So they hired a guy named Dave to write up the specification

Dave wasn't a CEO, or VC, or thought leader in this space. He was just a Phoenix employee hired after his last company went under. But unlike his last role, his task at this new company Phoenix wasn't to create anything new, or really create anything at all. It was to document thoroughly.

He was hired to rip off the big man himself, I - B - M.

IBM had a lot of software that a lot of people used, but in order to use that software, you needed an IBM compatible BIOS.


But IBM’s BIOS wasn’t just technical glue; it was a legal trap. Courts were beginning to accept that even behaviorally identical firmware could count as a copyrighted derivative if engineers had been exposed to the original code. Several clone makers had already been sued, settled, or quietly disappeared—not because their machines failed, but because their software was too similar.

Compatibility had become dangerous.

Everyone needed IBM compatibility to integrate with their popular software, but knew that reimplementing was a surefire way to get worked over by their lawyers.  Phoenix had some new ideas about how to skirt the rules though.

Instead of asking how to copy IBM’s BIOS, they asked how to never see it at all—and still rebuild its behavior. They split knowledge, roles, and responsibility so aggressively that no single engineer ever crossed the legal boundary IBM was defending. Specifications flowed in one direction. Code flowed in another.

This wasn't smart engineering but rather legal gymnastics and it placed Phoenix—and one particular engineer—directly at the center of a legal and technical experiment that would define what “cleanroom” software engineering actually meant.
That engineer would be Dave. Now unlike Compaq or the other companies that got sued into oblivion for re-implementing the IBM BIOS, Dave here didn't bother with re-implementing.

He would instead become intimately familiar with the IBM BIOS and write a detailed specification of every component of it. He would look at how IBM applications interfaced with it, even in undocumented ways, and he would write that all down, without ever copying down any of the original code. Then Dave would hand that document over to his colleague. Who would read the specification and implement a new BIOS, without ever having even seen the original material, guaranteeing that copying would have been physically impossible.

This was no easy task for Dave and his colleague. It took months of back and forth... and from what we heard, a little blurring of the lines of what could and couldn't be shared between the "dirty" engineer and the "clean" engineer. Still, at the end Phoenix was able to have a fully IBM compatible BIOS that it could sell to its customers and it did. It took months and months of engineering work but they got it working.

This work was more impactful than you might think. The only reason you can buy a motherboard and plug and play into any system these days, a big reason for that was the work Dave and Phoenix has done. (ask the robot)

In December 2021, the software world discovered a critical vulnerability in Apache Log4j, a Java logging library that sat quietly underneath an enormous portion of the global software stack.

t was everywhere — embedded in enterprise applications, cloud platforms, vendor products, government systems, and internal services. If you were running Java at scale, you were almost certainly using it — often without knowing.
The vulnerability, later called Log4Shell, allowed remote code execution by getting a system to log a specially crafted string. No authentication. No exploit chain. Just logging user-controlled data could lead to full system compromise.

Even after fixes were released, real-world systems remained vulnerable because patches had to flow through vendors, rebuild pipelines, and downstream consumers.

Log4J wasn't just an issue of a terrible vulnerability that caused a lot of damage, it was an issue of the inherent structural risk that exists by interconnecting so much of our software in the way that open source does.

The logistical issues associated with open source aren't only relegated to code. Licensing regimes within officially open source packages (those licensed by OSI approved licenses) are not all the same. For instance, the copyleft provisions in the AGPL can have serious implications on SaaS providers creating proprietary solutions. AGPLs viral licensing techniques can be seriously dangerous depending on how it's utilised, leading to many companies banning this license.

And even then, when PRODUCING open source software, managing the actual copyright and enforcement is an absolute nightmare. The best tool organizations have is to have to physically and contractually sign over copyright from all the contributors to an organization. Without that, enforcement becomes significantly more difficult. This is used by foundations who hopefully, if they have the money, can represent the interests of those contributors, or more often, by corporations who can then use that copyright power to relicense the software at a later date. Tools such as CLAs create leverage for corporations to modify open source into something that works for them, that is a tool they can use to leverage workers and competition.
